Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.

The condition is characterized by intellectual disability, which can range from mild to severe; seizures (seizures); a small head size (<LOCATION>) or an unusually large head size (>head circumference). Other features that may be present include: A cleft palate (a split in the roof of the mouth) Abnormalities of the eyes, such as crossed eyes (strabismus), droopy eyelids (ptosis), or abnormally shaped pupils (anisocoria) An abnormal curvature of the spine (scoliosis) Short stature (stunted growth) Heart defects Hearing loss Low-set ears (ears positioned lower than normal on the head) Small hands and feet (microdactyly) Delayed development of motor skills, such As sitting up alone before walking Walking with wide-legged stance (gait ataxia) Severe muscle weakness (hypotonia) In addition, some people with this disorder have other health problems, including diabetes mellitus type II, kidney failure, liver disease, heart valve abnormalities, thyroid gland dysfunction, and respiratory distress syndrome during infancy. Some children with 1Q44 deletion syndrome develop autism spectrum disorders, learning disabilities, behavioral problems, speech delays, and cerebral palsy. Others do not show any signs of developmental delay or impairment beyond their average intelligence level. People with 2q35 duplication syndrome also experience cognitive impairments but tend to have milder forms of these conditions compared with those who carry only one copy of chromosome 2. These differences likely reflect variations in how genes related to brain function are expressed within each individual's cells rather than being caused by changes in specific genetic sequences themselves.

reference: 17-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 deficiencyis an inherited condition that affects male sexual development. People with this condition are genetically male and have testes, but do not produce enough testosterone. Most people with this condition are born with external genitalia that appear female. In some cases, the external genitalia are ambiguous or appear male but are abnormal in size and/or appearance. During puberty, people with this condition typically go on to develop male secondary sex characteristics, such as increased muscle mass, deepening of the voice, and development of male pattern body hair. 17-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 deficiency is caused by mutations in the HSD17B3 gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

The diagnostic process may include medical history review, physical exam, laboratory tests, imaging studies, and consultation with other health care providers. A genetic counselor can help explain the results of these tests in relation to risk for recurrence in future pregnancies. Medical History Review: Information about your family's medical history will be collected. Physical Exam: An examination by a pediatrician or another health care provider will look for signs of developmental delay, short stature, distinctive facial features, heart defects, kidney abnormalities, and other characteristics associated with this condition. Laboratory Tests: Blood and urine samples are often taken during an initial evaluation. These samples are sent to a lab where they are tested for certain conditions. Imaging Studies: X-rays of the hands and feet may show characteristic bone changes seen in people with this disorder. Consultation With Other Health Care Providers: Your child may need testing done by specialists such as a cardiologist, neurologist, endocrinologist, ophthalmologist, orthopedic surgeon, speech pathologist, audiologist, dietitian, social worker, psychologist, occupational therapist, physiotherapist, and others who have expertise related to specific body systems or functions. Genetic Testing: Chromosome analysis using fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) or array comparative genomic hybridization (<PERSON>) can detect deletions involving genes involved in growth and development. This type of test looks for small areas of missing DNA within chromosomes. In some cases, chromosomal rearrangements called translocations occur instead of actual deletions. Translocation involves parts of two different chromosomes swapping places without any loss of genetic material. However, individuals with translocations do not usually develop the same set of symptoms as those with deletions because only one copy of each affected gene needs to be lost. Therefore, it is important to distinguish between deletions and translocations when making a diagnosis. If you suspect that your child has been misdiagnosed, consult with a genetics professional before proceeding with additional testing. It is also possible that no single test will provide a definitive answer; therefore, multiple types of testing may be needed. For example, if FISH or array CGH detects a deletion but does not identify all of the deleted regions, more detailed analyses might be performed to confirm the extent of the deletion. Additionally, sometimes parents report having had their children evaluated by several doctors over time, resulting in conflicting diagnoses. When this occurs, it may take longer to reach a final conclusion. Although there is currently no cure for most inherited disorders, early intervention through therapies and support groups can improve outcomes. Parents should discuss treatment options with their childs doctor. Some organizations offer information and resources for families dealing with rare diseases. reference: What causes a 15q11.2 microdeletion? A 15q11.2 microdeletion may occur randomly for the first time in an affected person (a de novo mutation), or it may be inherited from a parent with the microdeletion. A blood test to look at the parents' chromosomes is needed to find out how the microdeletion occurred. When a 15q11.2 microdeletion occurs as a de novo mutation, it is due to a random error - either during the formation of a parent's egg or sperm cell, or very soon after conception (fertilization of the egg). A parent with the microdeletion has a 50% chance with each pregnancy to pass on the microdeletion. The features of 15q11.2 microdeletion occur because the deleted region of the chromosome contains several genes that are important for normal growth and development. It is not yet clear why there is a large range of features and severity among people with a 15q11.2 microdeletion, or why some people are unaffected.
